tip: 'Manquer à' is reversed like 'plaire': 'ma famille me manque' = my family is missing to me. The thing missed is the subject.
'Manquer' agrees with its subject: 'mes amis me manquent' (plural subject = plural verb).
Sympa is the everyday clip of sympathique – both mean nice or friendly. It still adds -s in the plural: 'des voisins sympas'.
Marron never adds -e or -s: it's really the word for chestnut, so 'les chaussures marron' stays flat even in the plural.
'Il me reste' = I have left (literally: there remains to me). Reverse construction like falloir: il me reste, il te reste.
Faire plaisir à someone = to please them, literally 'to make pleasure to'. The person shows up as lui (to him/her): ce cadeau lui fait plaisir.

target: Un sac à dos bleu marine.
tip: Colors usually agree, but two-word colors freeze: bleu marine stays invariable – des sacs bleu marine, no -s. Same with vert clair.

target: Elle prend du jus de pomme.
tip: French can't just say 'juice' – it needs a 'some': du jus = some juice. Drop the du and it's ungrammatical, unlike English.

target: Le jardin de mon voisin est joli.
tip: French has no apostrophe-s. 'My neighbor's garden' becomes 'le jardin de mon voisin' – literally 'the garden of my neighbor'.

target: Tu es parti sans dire au revoir.
tip: After sans, French uses the plain verb, not the -ing form: sans dire au revoir = without saying goodbye.
'Blanc' (m.) → 'blanche' (f.) = white. Some adjectives have irregular feminine forms.
French drops the article for jobs: sa femme est avocate, not 'une avocate'. You only add un/une once there's a description: c'est une bonne avocate.
Ça me dit = 'that appeals to me', literally 'it says to me'. Add bien for warmth: ça me dit bien = I'm really up for it.
With aimer, use les for things in general: j'aime les films = I like movies as a whole. English drops the 'the'; French keeps it.
Animé means lively or bustling, not 'animated': les rues sont animées describes busy, buzzing streets.
In negative sentences, un/une/des/du/de la all become 'de' (or d'): Je n'ai pas de voiture. Il n'y a pas de lait.
Some adjectives go before the noun (BANGS: Beauty, Age, Number, Goodness, Size): petit, grand, beau, bon, jeune, vieux, nouveau.
Color adjectives go after the noun and agree: une robe bleue, un pantalon bleu, des chaussures bleues.
'Leur' (their, singular) and 'leurs' (their, plural): leur fils, leurs enfants. 'Leur' doesn't change for gender.
Nationality adjectives are lowercase in French: français(e), anglais(e), espagnol(e). They agree in gender and number.

target: J'ai acheté une tarte aux pommes.
tip: French flavors things with à, not 'of': une tarte aux pommes is an apple tart. Aux is à + les – literally 'a tart with the apples.'

target: Il est parti très tôt ce matin.
english: He left very early this morning.
tip: 'Partir' uses 'être': il est parti. The past participle agrees: elle est partie, ils sont partis.
A few adjectives sit before the noun: les grands arbres = the tall trees. Size, age, and beauty words like grand usually lead.
'Ça me plaît' is the most common way to say 'I like it' in casual French. More natural than 'j'aime ça'.
'Tu me manques' literally = You are missing to me = I miss you. The person missed is the subject, the person feeling the lack is the indirect object.
With plaire, use indirect object pronouns: me (to me), te (to you), lui (to him/her), nous, vous, leur. The thing liked is subject.
When the subject (thing liked) is plural, plaire becomes 'plaisent': Ces chaussures me plaisent = I like these shoes.
Weather takes 'il fait', not 'il est': 'il fait froid' means it's cold. 'Il est froid' would be about a person being cold.
French has no word for 'o'clock': telling time is just 'il est' plus the hour. 'Il est une heure' is literally 'it is one hour,' where 'il' is a dummy subject that names nobody.
'Plaisent' is plural because 'ces fleurs' is plural. Plaire agrees with its subject (the thing liked).
